I.C.3: Manage third-party AI risk through policies, assessments and contracts

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Create policies for each stage of the AI life cycle
  • Run an AI inventory and find shadow AI
  • Evaluate and update existing policies (privacy, security, data governance, IP) for AI
  • Manage third-party risk through policies, assessments and contracts
  • Cover procurement, supply chain, HR and acceptable use

2I.C.1: Put policies in place for oversight and accountability at every life-cycle stage

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Create, so the depth is Create. The course has 3 practice questions on this indicator.

Running case

47 AI Uses, 9 Unregistered

  • Mei Tanaka's first AI inventory at Helios finds 47 AI uses
  • Nine were never registered: shadow AI in sales, support and recruiting
  • Ravi Menon is about to sign with Corvid Labs without an AI review
  • You must write the policies that would have caught both

Policy, Standard, Procedure: The Governance Stack

  • Policy: the rule and its reason, approved by leadership (for example, every AI use case is reviewed before use)
  • Standard: measurable requirements that meet the policy (risk tiers, required tests)
  • Procedure: the steps people follow (the intake form and approval route)
  • Records: evidence that the steps happened (approvals, test results, logs)
  • Oversight and accountability need an owner, an approver and a review date on every policy

Exam tip: A policy says what must happen; a procedure says how; records prove it.

Policies Stage by Stage

  • Intake and use-case review: is AI the right tool, and is it allowed?
  • Risk assessment: how risky, and what controls?
  • Ethics and design review: fairness, transparency and oversight designed in
  • Data sourcing and use: rights, quality and privacy before data are used
  • Build, test and validation: standards for development and required tests
  • Release and live monitoring: approval gates, thresholds and owners
  • Records and incident response: documentation, reporting and escalation

Exam tip: For a stage question, name the control that belongs to that stage; do not borrow a later stage's control.

Intake and Use-Case Assessment

  • Every use case enters through one door, whether built, bought or switched on in a tool
  • Assess the purpose, the data, the affected people and the legal context
  • Tier the risk so that review is proportionate
  • Decide: go, no-go, or go with conditions; NIST expects the mapping to inform an initial go or no-go decision
  • Register the approved use in the inventory

Exam tip: The earliest control is the use-case gate; it stops problems before money and data are spent.

Risk Management and Ethics by Design

  • Risk policy: a method to identify, rate and treat risks, linked to the organization's risk tolerance (GOVERN 1.3)
  • Risk is tiered: more review for systems that affect people's rights, safety or access
  • Ethics by design: build fairness, explainability, privacy and human oversight into requirements, not bolt them on
  • Document risks and impacts of what teams design and use, and share them (GOVERN 4.2)
  • Culture: policies that foster critical thinking and a safety-first mindset (GOVERN 4.1)

Exam tip: Ethics by design means decisions made at design time, with a record, not a review at the end.

Data, Development, Training and Testing Policies

  • Data sourcing and use: lawful rights, license terms, consent and notice, minimization, quality checks and provenance records
  • Build standards: approved tools and libraries, version control for code, data and models, secure development
  • Training rules: which data may train which model, and who approves
  • Testing requirements: performance, robustness, security and bias tests with pass criteria
  • NIST asks for practices that enable AI testing, incident identification and information sharing (GOVERN 4.3)

Exam tip: If data were not cleared for use, no later test makes the model compliant.

Release, Monitoring, Records and Incidents

  • Release approval: a gate that checks test results, documentation and sign-off by the accountable owner
  • Live monitoring: metrics, thresholds, owners and review frequency (GOVERN 1.5)
  • Records: model documentation, decision logs and reports, kept for the period the policy sets
  • Incident response: report, triage, escalate, fix, learn; a named owner and timelines
  • Retirement: processes to decommission or phase out systems safely (GOVERN 1.7)

Exam tip: The life cycle ends with retirement; a policy set with no decommissioning step is incomplete.

The AI Inventory and Shadow AI Beyond the BoK

  • Inventory: a living list of every AI system and use, its owner, purpose, data and risk tier (NIST GOVERN 1.6)
  • Shadow AI: AI used without approval, from free web tools to features switched on inside existing software
  • Why it matters: you cannot govern, assess or retire what you cannot see
  • Finding it: surveys, network and expense data, procurement records, and an amnesty to report
  • Helios: 9 of 47 uses were unregistered; policy now requires registration at intake

Exam tip: An inventory is the first control; the fix for shadow AI is intake plus visibility, not only a ban.

3I.C.2: Check existing policies and update them for AI

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Evaluate, so the depth is Evaluate. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Reviewing Existing Policies for AI

  • Method: list existing policies, test each against AI risks, record the gaps, then decide to update or write a new policy
  • Privacy: training use, inferences and automated decisions are not covered
  • Security: model theft, data poisoning and prompt injection are not covered
  • Data governance: training-data provenance and dataset documentation are not covered
  • IP: rights in training data and outputs, and open-source terms, are not covered

Exam tip: Evaluating a policy means checking it against AI-specific risks, not rewriting it from scratch.

Updating Privacy and Security Policies for AI

Policy What to add for AI
Privacy purpose and notice for using personal data to train and run models; minimization; handling rights requests for data inside models; limits on sensitive inferences
Security AI-specific threats (data poisoning, model theft and extraction, prompt injection); access control for models and data; testing and red teaming; supply-chain checks of models and components
  • Treat model files, prompts and training data as assets to classify and protect
  • Link the incident process so that AI incidents reach security and privacy teams

Exam tip: An AI update extends the existing policy with AI-specific rules; the old controls still apply.

Updating Data Governance and IP Policies for AI

Policy What to add for AI
Data governance provenance and lineage of training data; quality and representativeness checks; dataset documentation; retention and deletion; who may use data for AI
Intellectual property rights to use data and content for training; ownership and use of outputs; open-source and model licenses; protection of prompts and confidential data in external tools
  • Add an acceptable use rule: no confidential or personal data in unapproved tools
  • Review the policies when systems, laws or incidents change, on a set schedule

Exam tip: Provenance and licenses are the first questions to ask about any training data.

4I.C.3: Manage third-party AI risk through policies, assessments and contracts

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Create, so the depth is Create. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Why Third-Party AI Risk Is Different

  • Most organizations buy or build on others' models, data and components
  • You inherit their data quality, bias, security and legal exposure
  • Suppliers can change a model without telling you
  • NIST names untraceable third-party components and poor supplier vetting as a generative-AI risk (value chain and component integration)
  • GOVERN 6.1 asks for policies for AI risks tied to third parties, including infringement of their IP or other rights

Exam tip: Buying AI does not buy the risk away; the organization using the system still owns its outcomes.

Third-Party Due Diligence and Assessments

  • Identify every third-party AI source, including free tools and embedded features
  • Tier by what the system does and the data it touches
  • Assess with evidence matched to the tier: documentation, test and bias results, data provenance, security and privacy controls, incident history
  • Contract the findings into obligations
  • Monitor and reassess on change or incident; plan the exit

Exam tip: Due diligence is proportionate: more evidence for higher-risk uses.

Procurement and Supply Chain Policies

  • No AI purchase without review: procurement routes every AI request through the intake gate
  • Approved suppliers and tools: a list of vetted vendors and models, with conditions of use
  • Standard questionnaire and clauses: the same questions and the same minimum terms for each bid
  • Supply-chain mapping: know which models, data and components sit under the vendor's product
  • Contingency plans: for failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems that are high-risk (GOVERN 6.2)

Exam tip: Procurement is a control point: if AI can enter without review, the intake policy fails.

AI Contract Terms Beyond the BoK

  • Data use: limits on training on your data, confidentiality
  • IP and indemnity: who owns outputs, who covers infringement claims
  • Transparency and documentation: what the vendor must disclose
  • Audit rights, incident notice, change notice: you hear about problems and model changes
  • Performance and exit: service levels and data return
  • For high-risk systems the AI Act (Article 25) requires a written agreement between provider and supplier on information, capabilities, technical access and assistance
  • Module 12 goes deeper on vendor agreements

Exam tip: Contract terms turn findings into duties; a risk found in diligence but left out of the contract is unmanaged.

HR and Acceptable Use Policies

  • Acceptable use of AI at work: approved tools, no confidential or personal data in unapproved ones, human review of outputs, disclosure where required
  • HR policies: how AI may be used in hiring, monitoring and performance decisions; training duties; consequences of misuse
  • Contractors and partners: the same rules in their agreements
  • Reporting: a safe way for staff to raise concerns or report incidents
  • Helios: recruiters may use the hiring tool only after training, and no candidate data may go into public chat tools

Exam tip: Staff are a source of third-party risk too: the quickest data leak is an employee pasting data into an unapproved tool.

Keeping Third-Party Risk Under Control

  • Reassess on triggers: a new model version, a new use, an incident, a change of supplier terms
  • Monitor: vendor performance, complaints, incident reports and audit findings
  • Keep records: assessments, approvals, contracts and exceptions in one place
  • Report up: third-party AI risk is a standing item for the AI governance committee
  • Exit plan: how to switch suppliers, retrieve data and retire dependencies

Exam tip: Third-party review is a cycle, not a one-time gate at signature.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Helios's first inventory finds nine AI uses that nobody had registered. Which policy change best addresses the cause?

  • ABan generative AI tools across the company until the next annual policy review cycle
  • BAsk each business unit to self-report its AI use once a year in a short internal survey
  • CRequire each AI use case to pass intake and risk tiering, then enter a central inventory
  • DAdd one sentence about AI use to the annual code of conduct acknowledgment that staff sign
Show the answer

Answer: C. Unregistered AI appears when there is no single door for new use cases. An intake gate with tiering and a central inventory makes AI visible and reviewed. A ban drives use underground, an annual survey is too slow, and a code-of-conduct line creates no process.

S2A company wants its strongest controls in place before any model is built. Which TWO policies matter most at that stage? (Select TWO.)

  • AA policy for decommissioning retired models and their data
  • BA use-case assessment and intake policy with a go or no-go decision
  • CAn incident-response policy with escalation timelines for live systems
  • DA data sourcing and use policy covering rights, quality and provenance
  • EA monitoring policy with drift thresholds for deployed systems
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. Before a build, the use case must be assessed and approved, and the data must be cleared for use. Decommissioning, incident response and monitoring apply to later stages of the life cycle.

S3An organization has policies for data, development and testing but none for what happens after launch. Which addition best closes the gap in oversight and accountability?

  • AMonitoring thresholds, an incident-escalation path and a named owner for every live system
  • BA second round of testing before each release, using a larger and much newer test dataset
  • CA requirement to publish the full source code of the deployed models to the general public
  • DA rule that training data must be deleted as soon as a model has been released to users
Show the answer

Answer: A. After launch, accountability depends on monitoring against thresholds, a route for escalating incidents and an owner for each live system. More pre-release testing, publishing source code or deleting training data does not give ongoing oversight.

S4A company's privacy policy covers customer data collected for service. It now wants to train a model on customer support chats. Which update is most needed?

  • ANone, because the existing policy already covers the use of customer data, wherever it occurs
  • BReplace the policy with the model vendor's standard terms of service covering the data
  • CLimit the update to the encryption standards used for storing the chat transcripts at rest
  • DRules on using personal data to train and run models: purpose, notice and rights requests
Show the answer

Answer: D. Training on personal data raises purpose, notice, minimization and rights-request questions the old policy did not address. The existing policy needs AI-specific additions, not replacement by vendor terms or a narrow encryption fix.

S5A review of an existing security policy for AI should conclude which of the following?

  • AThe policy is sufficient, because an AI system is just another application to protect
  • BThe policy should add AI-specific threats: data poisoning, model theft and prompt injection
  • CThe policy should drop access controls for models, because models are statistical objects
  • DThe policy should be replaced by the privacy policy, because AI risk is mainly about personal data
Show the answer

Answer: B. Existing controls still apply, but AI adds threats that a generic policy does not name, such as poisoned training data, theft or extraction of models and prompt injection. Evaluating the policy means finding and closing those gaps.

S6Ravi Menon is about to buy an AI tool for Helios. Which due-diligence step best manages third-party AI risk before signing?

  • ARely on the vendor's marketing material and the reputation of its other well-known customers
  • BAsk for price, support hours and delivery dates, then negotiate a larger volume discount
  • CTier the vendor by risk, then request evidence on documentation, testing and security to match
  • DAccept the vendor's standard terms unchanged to avoid delaying the purchase for the business teams
Show the answer

Answer: C. Due diligence is proportionate to risk: tier the use, then collect evidence on documentation, testing, data provenance and security. Marketing claims, price-only questions and unchanged standard terms leave the risk unassessed and uncontracted.

S7Which TWO contract terms best manage the risk that a vendor changes its AI model without warning? (Select TWO.)

  • AA duty to notify the buyer of material changes to the model, data or behavior
  • BA right for the vendor to train on customer data without a limit or a review step
  • CA disclaimer of warranties about the system's performance, accuracy and fitness
  • DAn automatic renewal of the agreement for several years without a review point
  • EA right to documentation and audit, so the buyer can reassess
Show the answer

Answer: A, E. Notice of material change lets the buyer know that the system moved, and documentation and audit rights let the buyer reassess it. Unlimited training rights, a warranty disclaimer and long auto-renewal add risk rather than reduce it.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Stack policy, standard, procedure, records; each with an owner and review date
Stages a policy topic for each life-cycle stage, from intake to retirement
Inventory list every AI use; shadow AI is found, not just banned
Existing policies test privacy, security, data governance and IP policies for AI gaps, then update
Third parties due diligence by tier, contract terms, procurement gate, acceptable use, ongoing review
